sentences.text: Serendipaceratops is a genus of herbivorous ornithischian dinosaur from the early Cretaceous of Australia that may be an ankylosaur.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, is a single ulna measuring about sixteen centimetres in length.
This bone features a broken olecranon process at the rear top and a flattened shaft.
The first bone was discovered in 1993 near Kilcunda on the south-east coast of Victoria, Australia, during the Dinosaur Cove project at the base of a cliff face.
The fossil was excavated in the "Arch", a small area of sea floor protected from waves by a dam.
The discoverers initially did not consider the fossil might be ceratopsian, as they did not expect to find evidence of that group in Australia.
Instead, the team initially tried to convince themselves the bone belonged to a theropod.
Colleague Dale Russell later pointed out the ulna's striking similarity to that of the primitive ceratopsian Leptoceratops.
The genus Serendipaceratops was named by Rich and Vickers-Rich in 2003.
The type species of the genus Serendipaceratops is Serendipaceratops arthurcclarkei.
The specific name arthurcclarkei honors science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke.
Only one fossil occurrence of Serendipaceratops has been recorded.
Serendipaceratops is classified within the class Ornithischia and belongs to the parent group Ceratopsia.
A 2010 study suggested the ulna was more similar to the ankylosaur Minmi than to basal ceratopsians and lacked ceratopsian synapomorphies.
A study by Angolin et al. found the ulna lacked ceratopsian synapomorphies and was more generally similar to the ankylosaur Minmi.
A 2021 study classified Serendipaceratops as an ankylosaur due to the robust proportions of its deformed ulna.

The holotype dates to the early Aptian stage, approximately 115 million years ago, and Serendipaceratops lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 116 million years ago in the Aptian stage, in what is now Australia.
Serendipaceratops lived during the Aptian stage, from 121.4 to 119.57 million years ago.
A 2014 study argued the taxon is valid based on ulna proportions falling within ceratopsian morphospace.
